solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable copy, its numbering matching the numbers printed in it and the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Term linked to endless scrawl, and RIP possibly? It's not so terminal! (12, two words, apostrophe)

indicators.note: possibly says the combined letters are only one possible order, so they may be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: endless means the word scrawl loses its final letter

parts.note: taken as written, then cut short
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wry epitaph-style musing on handwriting: a term, a scrawl and a RIP, but nothing fatal about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' trims scrawl to SCRAW; with TERM and RIP, 'possibly' rearranges the lot. 'Terminal' plays on the deadly-sounding RIP: this affliction of the hand is painful but never fatal.
explanation.definitionFit: This hand cramp from too much handwriting is uncomfortable rather than deadly, hence 'not so terminal'.

clue.text: Maybe Scotch day shortened, weather fickle?

parts.note: Scotch is an example of whisky
Friday cut short is the abbreviation Fri
the sky can stand for the weather, as in a stormy sky

explanation.surface: A Scottish day of drinking cut short because the weather keeps changing.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjective is a Chambers rhyming compound for flighty or giddy behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Whisky-frisky is a dictionary word for flighty or giddy, a synonym of fickle.

clue.text: E.g. old bloodhound, hot in pursuit?

indicators.note: in places the letter for hot within the word for pursuit

parts.note: a race is a pursuit, a chase after a quarry or rival
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A hound of old, hot on the trail of its quarry.
explanation.definitionFit: A rache is an archaic word for a hunting dog that follows by scent, such as a bloodhound.

clue.text: Small group, a real laugh with last going to No. 1

indicators.note: the final letter of the word moves round to the front position

parts.note: a riot is someone or something hilarious, a real laugh

explanation.surface: A little gang finds it hilarious that the last one ends up first.
explanation.definitionFit: A trio is a group of three, a small band or set of people.

clue.text: King off the fizz, King retaining energy for sport

indicators.note: off says the letter for king is removed from the champagne name

parts.note: Krug is a famous champagne house, and fizz is slang for champagne
K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: retaining means the royal cipher holds the energy letter inside it

parts.note: GR, Georgius Rex, is the cipher of King George
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A king gives up champagne and another keeps his energy for a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' takes K from KRUG (a champagne, 'the fizz') leaving RUG; GR 'retaining' E gives GER. Rugger is British slang for rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugger is the informal British name for rugby union football, a sport.

clue.text: Fine instruments? Composer must have died for us

indicators.note: must have ... for frames a swap: one letter group must take another's place
for completes the swap, the death letter standing in place of us

parts.note: Strauss is a composer (Johann or Richard)
taken as written: the letters US in the composer's name
D is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A grim demand that a composer die so that we may have fine instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Must have died for us' tells you D replaces US in STRAUSS. Strads are Stradivarius violins, and the question mark admits 'fine' is a hint, not a strict synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Strads, violins made by Stradivari, are among the finest stringed instruments ever made.

clue.text: Fix upper limit on e.g. car modelled with bloke around

indicators.note: around says the word for bloke goes round the rearranged letters

parts.note: a chap is a bloke, a man

indicators.note: modelled means shaped afresh, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written: the letters EGCAR

explanation.surface: Someone modelling a car with a bloke standing round wants to cap its price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modelled' reshapes 'e.g. car' into ARGEC, and the bloke goes 'around' it. Charge-capping was the British government limiting what local councils could levy.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge-cap is to impose a ceiling on what a local authority may levy, setting a maximum.

clue.text: Glimpse person collared by a copper

indicators.note: collared by means held round the neck, so the word sits inside the other letters

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
PER is short for person, as in grammar

explanation.surface: A quick look at someone being arrested by a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: PER is 'collared by' A and CU. Copper suggests a police officer, which fits 'collared', but here it is the metal's symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperçu is a brief insight or glimpse, a quick summary view.

clue.text: Arabesque is caught in dancing room

indicators.note: in puts the other letters inside the rearranged ones
dancing letters move about, so the word room is jumbled

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A decorative flourish captured in a ballroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing' makes MORO of room, and IS with C (caught) goes 'in' it. Morisco also names the morris dance, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Morisco means Moorish in style, which is what arabesque decoration or dance evokes.

clue.text: All women getting happiest (mostly) when excited about features of parapsychology (12, two words)

indicators.note: excited about means the letters are stirred up and rearranged

parts.note: if all are women there are no men, giving NO MEN

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of happiest is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then cut short

explanation.surface: An all-female group grows giddy with excitement about the paranormal.
explanation.walkthrough: All women means 'no men', NOMEN; 'mostly' cuts happiest to HAPPIES, and 'excited about' rearranges both together.
explanation.definitionFit: Psi phenomena are the telepathy and other paranormal effects studied by parapsychologists.

clue.text: E.g. fringe publish campaign's opener in shed

indicators.note: in places the publishing word and the opening letter inside the shed

parts.note: a hut is a shed
to air something is to make it public

indicators.note: opener means the first letter of campaign's

parts.note: first letter of campaign's

explanation.surface: A fringe campaign launched from a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: The opener of campaign's is C; AIR and C go 'in' HUT. Fringe seems to mean a political fringe, but it is the hair cut across the forehead.
explanation.definitionFit: A fringe is a style of trimming the front hair, so it is one kind of haircut.

clue.text: Syringes creating nervy attitude, we hear?

indicators.note: we hear means the answer is said like the words for a nervy attitude

parts.note: high (on edge, overexcited) plus pose (an attitude) gives HIGH POSE

explanation.surface: Needles that make the patient adopt a tense stance.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypo is short for hypodermic, the hollow needle used for injections.

clue.text: System to aid future planning? Irritation when time is lost (6, two words)

indicators.note: is lost means the time letter drops out of the word

parts.note: itching is an irritation of the skin

explanation.surface: A planning method that loses time to petty irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: T 'is lost' from ITCHING. The I Ching is an ancient Chinese book consulted for divination.
explanation.definitionFit: The I Ching is used for divination, foretelling what is to come, so it helps plan ahead.

clue.text: Knack, one which anglers have at heart

indicators.note: have at heart says the letters sit in the middle of these words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of which and the start of anglers

explanation.surface: Anglers' secret skill, something they hold dear.
explanation.definitionFit: To get the hang of something is to acquire the knack of doing it.

clue.text: Pa quitting procession travelled up north

indicators.note: quitting means the letters of Pa leave the word

parts.note: a parade is a procession

explanation.surface: Father drops out of the march and heads north.
explanation.walkthrough: PA 'quitting' PARADE leaves the answer. 'Up north' marks the Scots form: rade is the Scots past tense of ride.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, rade means rode, the past tense of ride, so it means journeyed.

clue.text: What ministers show: latitude, fine in business centre

indicators.note: in puts the latitude letter and the fine inside the business centre

parts.note: the City is London's financial district
an eric was a fine paid for murder under old Irish law

explanation.surface: Ministers granted leeway and fined in the City.
explanation.walkthrough: Ministers looks political but means clergy. An eric is a blood-fine in early Irish law.
explanation.definitionFit: Clericity is the condition of being a cleric, which clergy display.

clue.text: Ditch job in Oz, good split

definitions.meaning: a grip is a dialect word for a small ditch or drain
in Australian slang a grip is a job

parts.note: to rip is to split or tear

explanation.surface: An Australian digging job that paid well before the team split up.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions share the wordplay; Oz is Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Grip means both a narrow trench and, in Australian slang, a job or occupation.

clue.text: Anchor securing net at sea with line as ballast

indicators.note: securing means the anchor holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: a kedge is a small anchor

indicators.note: at sea means confused, so the word net is rearranged

explanation.surface: A boat drops anchor with its net and lines as ballast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' jumbles net into ENT, and with the line letter it sits after the anchor's first letter, the anchor 'securing' it. A kedge is a small anchor used for warping a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentledge is pig iron or scrap carried as permanent ballast in a ship's hold.

clue.text: A grey gee transported Scottish pedlar

indicators.note: transported means moved about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
gee is the spelt-out name of the letter G

explanation.surface: A travelling pedlar carried along by a grey horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transported' rearranges A, GREY and G. Gee looks like a horse (gee-gee), which suits the pedlar, but it is the letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: Yagger is a Scots word for a hawker or travelling seller.

clue.text: Some dragonflies chase flies — name one

indicators.note: flies means moves wildly, so the word chase is rearranged

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, one

explanation.surface: An instruction to identify a dragonfly as it chases flies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flies' looks like insects the dragonflies chase, but it is the anagram signal turning chase into AESCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeschna is a genus of large hawker dragonflies, so it covers a group of them.

clue.text: Allure and experience surrounding Wellington, according to Boney?

indicators.note: surrounding means the experience word goes around the title

parts.note: to see something is to experience it
Napoleon (Boney) would call the Duke of Wellington le Duc in French

explanation.surface: Napoleon's view of Wellington's charm and experience.
explanation.walkthrough: SEE goes 'surrounding' DUC: Boney is Napoleon, who would speak of the Duke in French as 'duc'.
explanation.definitionFit: To allure someone is to tempt or entice them, as does seduce.

clue.text: Bones: look for them buried in Roman marketplaces

indicators.note: buried in means placed inside the marketplaces

parts.note: fora is the Latin plural of forum, a Roman marketplace
'em is a colloquial short form of them

explanation.surface: An archaeologist's tip: dig for bones under Roman forums.
explanation.definitionFit: Femora is the plural of femur, the thigh bone.

clue.text: Individual in Highland festival with lunar decoration?

indicators.note: in places the single person inside the festival

parts.note: the Mod is a Scottish Gaelic festival of music and literature
one is a single individual

explanation.surface: A solo performer at a Gaelic festival wearing moon motifs.
explanation.definitionFit: Mooned can describe something ornamented with crescent or moon shapes.

clue.text: Chaps in 'eadgear, one displaying tufty parts

indicators.note: in places the chaps inside the headgear

parts.note: headgear with the h dropped, as cockneys do, is a hat with no h
men are chaps
A is the article, one

explanation.surface: Men in cockney hats, one sporting tufts.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe marks the dropped h, so the hat is just AT; MEN go 'in' it for AMENT, then A.
explanation.definitionFit: Amenta are catkins, the hanging fluffy flower spikes of willow and hazel.

clue.text: Metrical form, hybrid, having to conform to its rules outwardly?

indicators.note: having means the conforming word holds the hybrid
outwardly says that word sits on the outside

parts.note: verse that scans conforms to the rules of metre
a zo is a yak-cow hybrid in the Himalayas

explanation.surface: A verse form, a mongrel, that must keep to its own outer rules.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanning word is 'having' the hybrid, sitting 'outwardly' round it. A zo (also dzo or zho) is a cross between a yak and a cow; 'its rules' points back to the metrical form.
explanation.definitionFit: A scazon is a limping iambic line ending with a spondee or trochee, a type of verse metre.

clue.text: One colt has raced round, given a kick?

indicators.note: round means the racing word goes round the other letters

parts.note: sped means raced
I is the Roman numeral one
C is the abbreviation for colt in racing form

explanation.surface: A young horse runs a lap and gets kicked.
explanation.walkthrough: SPED goes 'round' I and C. 'Kick' looks like a horse's blow, but it is the zing of spice.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiced food has been given a kick, a strong or pungent flavour.

clue.text: On quitting Jerusalem, Italian consumed pasta

indicators.note: consumed means the shortened word swallows the Italian letters
quitting means the letters of on leave the word

parts.note: Zion is a name for Jerusalem

explanation.surface: An Italian leaving Jerusalem eats pasta.
explanation.walkthrough: ON 'quitting' ZION leaves ZI, which has 'consumed' IT. Zion is a biblical name for Jerusalem.
explanation.definitionFit: Ziti is a tube-shaped pasta from southern Italy.

clue.text: Congenial

parts.note: this was the competition clue: the setter gives only a definition and readers compose their own clues for the word

explanation.walkthrough: In an Azed competition puzzle one entry is clued by its bare definition, and solvers are invited to write a clue for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Simpatico, borrowed from Italian and Spanish, describes someone likeable and easy to get on with.

clue.text: Give way, almost, on cutting in, indicating diversion?

indicators.note: cutting in means the word on enters the yielding word
almost means the last letter is left off

parts.note: to cede is to give way

explanation.surface: A traffic scene: nearly yielding, someone cuts in and a diversion is signed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts CEDE to CED, and ON comes 'cutting in'. A coned road has traffic cones placed to divert or close lanes.
explanation.definitionFit: A road that is coned off has cones marking a diversion or closed lane.

clue.text: Magic one conceals this sprite maybe

indicators.note: conceals means the answer lies within these words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of magic and the start of one

explanation.surface: A magic spell hides a fairy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Magic one conceals' the answer across its two words. Sprite seems to mean a fairy, but a sprite is also a small graphic on a computer screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprite in computing is a small graphic image, like a desktop icon.

clue.text: Starts to mature after teenage years — too familiar?

indicators.note: starts to means take the first letter of each of these words

parts.note: the opening letters of mature, after, teenage and years

explanation.surface: A person growing up after the teens who becomes overly friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: Maty means friendly, sometimes overly so, being pally with others.

clue.text: Scots own highland region whence river emerges

indicators.note: emerges means the river letter comes out of the region name

parts.note: Nairn is a town and former county in the Scottish Highlands

explanation.surface: A Scot's own Highland district, source of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: R 'emerges' from NAIRN, a town in the Scottish Highlands. Nain is the Scots form of own.
explanation.definitionFit: Nain is a Scots dialect word meaning own, as in 'my nain'.

clue.text: Polished ——? May be seen in Daphnis and Chloe, i.e. spinning

definitions.text: Polished ——? May be seen in Daphnis and Chloe, i.e. spinning

parts.words: Polished ——? May be seen in Daphnis and Chloe, i.e. spinning
parts.note: a ballet step of rapid spinning turns, which dancers aim to make polished, would appear in Ravel's ballet about the two lovers

explanation.surface: A ballet critic praising a smooth turn in Ravel's ballet.
explanation.walkthrough: Daphnis and Chloe is Ravel's ballet, where such steps would be danced; the gap invites the phrase for a well executed turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaîne is a ballet movement of quick linked turns across the stage, a form of spinning.

clue.text: Herd drunk? Not I. I deferred maybe

indicators.note: not I means the letter I is removed, once from each of the two words

parts.note: kine is an old plural of cow, a herd of cattle
the letter I, removed here and again from the next word
lit is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: A sober refusal: the herd may be drunk, but not me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not I' takes an I out of both KINE and LIT, leaving KNE and LT.
explanation.definitionFit: Kneeling is a gesture of deference, so 'I knelt' could describe an act of respect.

clue.text: Adherents of the Good Book garbled extent, introducing mass

indicators.note: introducing means the mass letter is inserted into the jumbled letters
garbled means mixed up, so extent is rearranged

explanation.surface: Bible readers garble the extent of the text at Mass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garbled' turns extent into TEXTEN, with M 'introducing' itself after TEXT.
explanation.definitionFit: Textmen are those who quote scripture text closely, strict adherents of the Bible.

clue.text: Tiresome chat recalling one period over and over again (12, three words)

indicators.note: recalling means calling back, so the words are read backwards

parts.note: A is the article, one
a day is a period of time
the same backwards day repeated twice more

explanation.surface: Boring talk that goes over the same day again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalling' reads A DAY backwards as YADA, and 'over and over again' repeats it twice more.
explanation.definitionFit: Yada yada yada is slang for tedious, empty talk, blah blah blah.
